A Zn-Al-Si-based plated layer is provided in which both the chemical composition and the internal metallographic structure of the coating are carefully controlled. The plated layer contains zinc, aluminum, and silicon as principal components, with the respective contents defined in mass percent so that the coating forms a desired solidification structure after plating. In addition to the plated layer itself, an intermetallic compound layer is formed at the interface between the plated layer and the underlying steel substrate. This intermetallic compound layer is also controlled, particularly with respect to its thickness, so that it does not grow excessively and adversely affect the properties of the coating.

The microstructure of the Zn-Al-Si-based plated layer includes a plurality of characteristic phases and structural regions. These include Al-Zn first structures, eutectoid structures, Zn-rich phases, and intermetallic compound phases. By regulating the distribution and area fraction of these structures within the plated layer, the coating can be made more uniform and stable. The Al-Zn first structures contribute to the overall solidification morphology of the plated layer, while the eutectoid structures and Zn-rich phases influence the balance of corrosion resistance, appearance, and mechanical behavior. The intermetallic compound phases, meanwhile, are controlled so that they remain within an appropriate range and do not impair coating adhesion or formability.

A key feature of the plated steel material is that the area fractions of these microstructural components are specified within defined limits. This makes it possible to obtain a plating layer having a consistent and reproducible structure, rather than one in which coarse or uneven phases are randomly distributed. Such control is important because variations in phase distribution can lead to differences in coating performance, including corrosion resistance, surface quality, cracking resistance, and adhesion during forming or processing.

The intermetallic compound layer formed between the steel substrate and the Zn-Al-Si-based plated layer is controlled to a thickness of 2 μm or less. Keeping this layer thin is significant because an excessively thick intermetallic layer can become brittle and may reduce the ability of the coating to withstand bending, pressing, or other deformation. A thin and uniform intermetallic compound layer improves the bonding between the substrate and the plated layer while helping to maintain good workability.

Through the combined control of composition, phase area fractions, and interfacial intermetallic layer thickness, the plated layer achieves a tightly regulated coating structure. This controlled structure is significant for ensuring stable coating quality and consistent performance across the plated steel product. As a result, the material can exhibit reliable corrosion resistance, good coating adhesion, and improved durability during subsequent manufacturing and use.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest and most common words in the English language, yet it plays an important role in communication. It is called a definite article, and it helps us point to something specific. For example, when we say “a book,” we may mean any book. But when we say “the book,” we are referring to a particular book that the speaker and listener both understand.

This simple word gives clarity and direction to sentences. It can make an idea feel more certain, important, or unique. Phrases like “the sun,” “the world,” and “the truth” show how “the” can introduce concepts that feel universal or well-known.

Although “the” is easy to overlook, it is essential in everyday speech and writing. Without it, many sentences would sound incomplete or confusing. In this way, “the” proves that even the smallest words can have great meaning.

1. **A Zn—Al—Si—Mg plated steel material** comprising a steel substrate and a hot-dip plated layer disposed on at least one surface of the steel substrate,  

wherein the plated layer has a chemical composition comprising, by mass percent based on a total mass of the plated layer:  

- Al: **4.0% to 22.0%**,  
- Mg: **1.0% to 8.0%**,  
- Si: **0.05% to 2.0%**,

- an Al-rich phase having an area fraction of **5% to 60%**,  
- an Mg-containing intermetallic phase including at least one of MgZn₂, Mg₂Zn₁₁, or an Mg—Zn—Al ternary eutectic constituent, the Mg-containing intermetallic phase having an area fraction of **5% to 45%**, and  
- an Si-containing phase including at least one of Mg₂Si, elemental Si, or an Al—Fe—Si compound, the Si-containing phase having an area fraction of **0.1% to 10%**,

wherein a maximum thickness of the Fe—Al intermetallic alloy layer is **10.0 μm or less**, and  

wherein the plated layer has a coating weight of **20 g/m² to 300 g/m² per side**.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a technical paragraph in patent language defining the chemical composition and microstructure requirements of a plating layer and intermetallic compound layer for an aluminum-zinc based coated steel sheet.
counterfactuals.output: In one embodiment, an aluminum-zinc based coated steel sheet comprises a steel substrate, a plating layer formed on at least one surface of the steel substrate, and an intermetallic compound layer interposed between the steel substrate and the plating layer. The plating layer comprises, by mass percent, Al: 45 to 75%, Zn: 20 to 55%, Si: 0.1 to 5.0%, Mg: 0 to 10%, and inevitable impurities, with the balance being Zn and/or Al depending on the target alloy phase constitution, wherein the plating layer has a microstructure including an aluminum-rich dendritic phase and a zinc-rich interdendritic phase, and optionally an Mg-containing phase selected from MgZn₂, Mg₂Si, and Al—Mg—Zn based compounds. The plating layer is preferably controlled such that coarse oxide inclusions and brittle eutectic segregates are suppressed, an average dendrite arm spacing is 1 to 30 μm, and a surface region thereof contains no continuous brittle phase extending in a thickness direction of the coating. The intermetallic compound layer comprises an Fe—Al based compound containing at least one of Zn and Si, and includes one or more phases selected from Fe₂Al₅, FeAl₃, FeAl₂, and Fe—Al—Si based compounds. The intermetallic compound layer has an average thickness of 0.05 to 5.0 μm, preferably 0.1 to 2.0 μm, and is formed substantially continuously along the interface between the steel substrate and the plating layer while being limited so as not to form coarse tongue-like projections penetrating into the plating layer. The intermetallic compound layer preferably contains Si in an amount effective to suppress excessive growth of Fe—Al intermetallics, and has a thickness variation, defined as a maximum thickness divided by an average thickness, of not more than 5.0, thereby providing improved adhesion, corrosion resistance, and workability of the aluminum-zinc based coated steel sheet.
